audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Tryon 1968 passage is verbatim in the held at printed pp. 1-2 (pp. 13-14), and the p. 2 examples (/émakàn/, /máhiñèn/, /húčučè/ = 101; /bárakòñɛn/ = 1010) match the catalog string stress placement coded per word length as 10 101 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable); StressTyp2's own passage for the StressTyp2 entry for this language quotes the same rule, so the recorded StressTyp2 contradiction (100 vs 101) is StressTyp2's slip, not ours. (2) Deciding source is a 1968 primary descriptive grammar; the fuller reference grammar is Ozanne-Rivierre 1976 (not yet obtained, print only), but Lynch 2002:777, which abstracts O-R 1976 and which we hold, states the identical primary-initial / secondary-final-in-trisyllables / secondary-penult-otherwise rule, so two independent descriptive lines agree. Dotte 2013 (downloaded now, 529 pp) is silent on accent. (3) Nothing found suggests the classification is wrong; the record's grade field is empty, so the action is to upgrade the evi

sources.quote: "1. Stress — In Iai, stress is non-phonemic. It is conditioned by the syllable and nuclear structure of the word. There are three degrees of stress in Iai: primary stress, secondary stress and unstress. These three degrees of stress occur as follows: (a) Primary Stress — Primary stress always occurs on the first syllable of the word. sources.quote: 'Primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word, while secondary stress occurs on the final syllable of trisyllabic words and on the penultimate syllable of words of more than three syllables.'
